draft.title: The distribution of sample means
card: Take many random samples of size n from a population with mean μ and standard deviation σ. Each sample has its own mean, written x̄. These sample means form a distribution.
The mean of the sample means is μ. Their standard deviation is σ/√n. A bigger sample gives a smaller spread, because √n is larger.
If the population is normal, x̄ is normal for any n. If not, x̄ is roughly normal when n is large. This is the central limit theorem.
Example: σ = 12 and n = 36. Then σ/√n = 12 ÷ 6 = 2. The sample means have a standard deviation of 2.
draft.remember: Sample means centre on μ, with spread σ/√n. Larger samples spread less.

a.q: A population has mean 50 and standard deviation 20. Samples of size 25 are taken. What is the standard deviation of the sample means?
a.why: The standard deviation is σ/√n = 20 ÷ √25 = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Using 20 ignores the sample size, which is a common mistake. That is the spread of single values, not of sample means.
a.clue: Divide σ by the square root of n, not by n.

b.q: Machine parts have a mean length of 80 mm and a standard deviation of 6 mm. Sample size is increased from 9 to 36. What happens to the standard deviation of the sample means?
opts: It halves, from 2 mm to 1 mm
It falls to a quarter, from 2 mm to 0.5 mm
It stays at 6 mm, as σ does not change
It halves, from 6 mm to 3 mm
b.why: For n = 9, 6/√9 = 2. For n = 36, 6/√36 = 1. Sample size rose by a factor of 4, so the spread falls by a factor of √4 = 2, not 4. The population σ stays at 6, but it is not the spread of sample means.
b.clue: Work out σ/√n for both sample sizes and compare.

b.best: It halves, from 2 mm to 1 mm
